---
title: "A scenario grid"
---

The district has to decide what to put in the next distribution. Five options are on the
table:

1. **Withdraw the nets.** There is no campaign at all. This is not a serious policy, but it
   is the counterfactual every other option is measured against. It is also the arm that
   results if the campaign is not restated.
2. **Replace like for like** with pyrethroid-only nets at the same 0.70 coverage.
3. **Switch to PBO**, again at 0.70.
4. **Switch to pyrrole**, again at 0.70.
5. **PBO plus IRS at 0.60 plus LSM at 0.30.** This is the most expensive package.

Every arm shares the same setting (prevalence 0.45, resistance 0.30, pyrethroid-only nets at
0.70 now) and therefore the same `EirTarget`. The baseline EIR is inverted from the same
prevalence under the same current net mix. All five scenarios therefore start from an
identical transmission intensity and an identical pre-campaign trajectory. Any difference
between them is caused by the campaign and nothing else.

## Building the grid

The shared fields go in a dictionary and are splatted into each `Scenario`. Only the
campaign is written out per arm.

```{python}
from estimint import run_scenarios
from estimint.scenarios import Scenario, EirTarget

district = dict(
    res_use=0.30,
    Q0=0.85,
    phi=0.80,
    seasonal=0.0,
    irs=0.0,
    py_only=0.70,     # the nets in place today
    routine=0.0,
    eir_target=EirTarget(0.45, "prevalence"),
)

grid = [
    Scenario(name="Withdraw", **district),
    Scenario(
        name="Pyrethroid-only",
        itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_only",
        **district,
    ),
    Scenario(
        name="PBO",
        itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pbo",
        **district,
    ),
    Scenario(
        name="Pyrrole",
        itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pyrrole",
        **district,
    ),
    Scenario(
        name="PBO + IRS + LSM",
        itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pbo",
        irs_future=0.60, lsm=0.30,
        **district,
    ),
]

len(grid)
```

If R is your first language, the dictionary-splat idiom is the Python equivalent of
`do.call(Scenario, c(district, list(name = "PBO", ...)))`. Use it rather than repeating the
shared fields five times over. A typo in one arm's `Q0` would silently break the comparison.

## One call

`run_scenarios` takes the list, loads the models once, and puts the five scenarios through
the emulator as a single batch. Five arms cost barely more than one.

```{python}
res = run_scenarios(grid)
res.shape
```

What comes back is five rows, one per arm, and the same twenty-three columns as before.

## The shared baseline

Check it before reading anything else. If the five arms did not start from the same place,
none of the comparisons that follow would mean anything.

```{python}
res[["name", "dn0_use", "itn_use", "eir_baseline", "prev_y9"]]
```

All five arms share the same `dn0_use`, the same `itn_use`, an `eir_baseline` of about 32
infectious bites per person per year, and a `prev_y9` of about 0.456 against the 0.45 that
went in. They are indistinguishable up to the campaign. They diverge only after it.

## The summary table

The campaign columns and the two endline outcomes are what the grid was built for.

```{python}
res[[
    "name", "net_future", "dn0_future", "itn_future",
    "irs_future", "lsm", "prev_endline", "cases_endline",
]]
```

Read the `dn0_future` column first. At resistance 0.30 a pyrethroid-only net kills about
0.31 of the mosquitoes that touch it, a PBO net about 0.48, and a pyrrole net about 0.55.
The ranking of the three net arms follows from that ordering and nothing else, since every
other covariate is held fixed.

The combination arm has the PBO `dn0_future` (the nets are the same nets) but adds spraying
at 0.60 and larviciding at 0.30 on top. The endline prevalence it reaches is an order of
magnitude below any net-only arm. Within nets, the product choice changes prevalence by a
few points. Adding a second and third vector-control measure changes it considerably
further. Whether the district can afford that is not a question the emulator answers.

## The withdrawal arm

The first row of the grid shows the values the defaults produce.

```{python}
res.loc[res["name"] == "Withdraw", ["net_future", "dn0_future", "itn_future", "irs_future"]]
```

`net_future` is `"none"`, `dn0_future` is 0, and `itn_future` is 0. That row was built by
passing the district dictionary and nothing else, with no `itn_future` and no
`net_type_future`. Those are the values the defaults supply.

If the campaign is not restated, the district has been modelled as stopping net distribution
altogether. No warning is raised. The call succeeds, the frame comes back, and the
trajectory is plausible. The only indication is the rebound, and it is obviously wrong only
to a reader who was expecting the nets to continue.

```{python}
import numpy as np

withdraw = res.loc[res["name"] == "Withdraw"].iloc[0]
like_for_like = res.loc[res["name"] == "Pyrethroid-only"].iloc[0]

float(withdraw["prev_endline"]), float(like_for_like["prev_endline"])
```

Here the withdrawal arm ends about one and a half prevalence points above like-for-like
replacement. The gap is small enough to be mistaken for noise by a reader who was not
looking for it. The difference in cumulative case burden between the two is considerably
larger, as [Comparing campaigns](comparing.qmd) works out.

Keep the arm deliberately. It is the counterfactual that makes "cases averted" a meaningful
quantity.
